source_text: Iam hinc ad quaestiones t omnes, o canes, quos foras apostolus expellit, latrantes in deum ueritatis. haec sunt argumentationum ossa, quae obroditis: (si deus bonus et praescius futuri et auertendi mali potens, cur hominem, et quidem imaginem et similitudinem suam, immo et substantiam suam, per animae scilicet censum, passus est labi de, obsequio legis in mortem, circumuentum a diabolo? si enim et bonus, qui euenire tale quid nollet, et praescius, qui euenturum non ignoraret, et potens, qui depellere ualeret, nullo modo euenisset quod sub his tribus condicionibus diuinae maiestatis euenire non posset. quod si euenit, absolutum est e contrario deum neque bonum credendum neque praescium neque potentem; siquidem in quantum nihil tale euenisset, si talis deus, id est bonus et praescius et potens, in tantum ideo euenit, quia non talis deus), ad haec prius est istas species in creatore defendere, quae in dubium uocantur, bonitatem dico et praescientiam et potentiam. nec immorabor huic articulo, praeeunte definitione etiam ipsius Christi ex operibus ineundae probationis. opera creatoris utrumque testantur, et bonitatem eius, qua bona, sicut ostendimus, et potentiam, qua tanta, et quidem ex nihilo. nam et si ex aliqua materia, ut quidam uolunt, hoc ipso tamen ex nihilo; dum non id fuerunt, quod sunt. postremo uel sic magna, dum bona, uel sic deus potens, dum omnia ipsius, unde et omnipotens. de praescientia uero quid dicam, quae tantos habet testes, quantos fecit prophetas? quamquam quis praescientiae titulus in omnium auctore. qui uniuersa utique (et) disponendo praesciit et praesciendo disposuit? certe ipsam transgressionem, quam nisi praescisset. nec cautionem eius delegasset sub metu mortis. igitur si et fuerunt in deo istae facultates, prae quibus nihil mali euenire homini aut potuisset aut debuisset, et nihilominus euenit. uideamus et hominis condicionem, ne per illam potius euenerit quod per deum euenire non potuit. liberum et sui arbitrii et suae potestatis inuenio hominem a deo institutum, nullam magis imaginem et similitudinem dei in illo animaduertens quam eiusmodi status formam. neque enim facie et corporalibus lineis, tam uariis in genere humano, ad uniformem deum expressus est, sed in ea substantia, quam ab ipso deo traxit, id est anima, ad formam dei, spondentis et arbitrii sui libertatem et potestatem, signatus est. hunc statum eius confirmauit etiam ipsa lex tunc a deo posita. non enim poneretur lex ei, qui non haberet obsequium debitum legi in sua potestate, nec rursus comminatio mortis transgressioni adscriberetur, si non et contemptus legis in arbitrii libertatem homini deputaretur. sic et in posteris legibus creatoris inuenias. proponentis ante hominem bonum et malum, uitam et mortem. sed nec alias totum ordinem disciplinae per praecepta dispositum a uocante deo, et minante et hortante, nisi et ad obsequium et ad contemptum libero et uoluntario homini.
pass_a_gloss: Now from here to all questions, O dogs, whom the apostle expels, barking against the God of truth. These are the bones of arguments, which you gnaw: (if God is good and prescient of the future and able to avert evil, why did He permit man, and indeed His image and likeness, and even His substance, through the soul's judgment, to slip away from obedience to the law into death, deceived by the devil? For if He is good, who would not wish such a thing to happen, and prescient, who would not be ignorant of what was going to happen, and able, who could drive it away, in no way would it have happened what under these three conditions of divine majesty could not happen. But if it happened, it is concluded on the contrary that God is not to be believed to be good or prescient or able; for to the extent that such a thing would not have happened if God were such, that is good and prescient and able, to that extent it happened because God is not such). To these things, it is first necessary to defend these species in the Creator, which are called into doubt, I say goodness and prescience and ability. Nor will I delay on this article, with the definition of Christ Himself preceding, to be begun from His works. The works of the Creator testify to both His goodness, by which He is good, as we have shown, and His ability, by which He is so great, and indeed from nothing. For even if from some matter, as some wish, nevertheless from nothing in this respect, since they were not what they are. Finally, either so great, since good, or so able, since God, while all things are His, whence also omnipotent. But what shall I say about prescience, which has as many witnesses as it has made prophets? Although what title of prescience is there in the author of all things, who certainly foreknows all things by disposing them and disposes them by foreknowing? Certainly He foreknew that very transgression, which unless He had foreknown, He would not have entrusted its caution under the fear of death. Therefore, if such faculties were in God, before which no evil could happen to man or should have happened, and nevertheless it happened. Let us see also the condition of man, lest it happened through that rather than through God what could not happen through God. I find man instituted by God free and of his own judgment and of his own power, noticing no image and likeness of God in him more than the form of such a status. For not by face and bodily lines, so varied in the human race, was he expressed to the uniform God, but in that substance which he drew from God Himself, that is the soul, to the form of God, promising and freedom of judgment and power, he was signed. This status of his was confirmed also by the law then placed by God. For the law would not be placed for him who did not have obedience to the law in his power, nor would the threat of death be ascribed to transgression, if contempt of the law were not also entrusted to man's freedom of judgment. So also in the later laws of the Creator you will find. He proposes good and evil, life and death, before man. Nor otherwise the whole order of discipline disposed through precepts by the calling God, and threatening and exhorting, unless to free and voluntary obedience and contempt of man.
pass_b_english: So let's turn to the questions, all of you—you dogs the apostle kicks out for barking against the God of truth. These are the bones of the arguments you gnaw on: If God is good, knows the future, and has the power to stop evil, why did He let man—His image and likeness, indeed His very substance through the soul’s judgment—slip from obedience to the law into death, tricked by the devil? If He is good, He would not want such a thing to happen; if He foresees, He would not be ignorant of it coming; if He is able, He could drive it away. Under those three conditions of divine majesty, the disaster could not have happened. But it did happen. Therefore, the opposite conclusion stands: God cannot be believed to be good, or prescient, or powerful. To the exact degree that such a thing would not have happened if God were truly good, prescient, and able, to that degree it happened because He is not such a God. So first we must defend these attributes in the Creator—goodness, prescience, and power—since they are the ones called into doubt. I will not linger here; Christ’s own definition leads the way, and the proof starts from His works. The Creator’s works testify to both His goodness—by which He is good, as we have shown—and His power, by which He is so great, and indeed created from nothing. Even if He used some pre-existing matter, as some claim, it still counts as creation from nothing, because those things were not what they are now. Ultimately, He is so great because He is good, and so powerful because He is God—all things are His, which is why He is called omnipotent. What about prescience? It has as many witnesses as there are prophets. What title to prescience could be greater than the Author of all things, who foreknows everything by disposing it and disposes everything by foreknowing it? He certainly foreknew that very transgression; otherwise He would not have entrusted its warning under the threat of death. So if these faculties existed in God—faculties before which no evil could or should have happened to man—and yet it happened anyway, let us examine man’s condition. Perhaps the disaster came through man rather than through God, since it could not come through God. I find that God instituted man as free, possessing his own judgment and his own power. I see no image and likeness of God in him more clearly than the form of that status. He was not expressed toward the uniform God by face and bodily lines, which vary so widely across the human race, but in that substance he drew from God Himself—the soul—he was sealed to the form of God, guaranteeing freedom of judgment and power. The law God then gave confirmed this status. Law would not be given to someone who did not have obedience to the law in his power, nor would the threat of death be attached to transgression if contempt for the law were not also entrusted to man’s freedom of judgment. You find the same pattern in the Creator’s later laws. He sets good and evil, life and death, before man. Nor is the whole order of discipline arranged through precepts by the calling, threatening, and exhorting God in any other way than to address a free and voluntary human being capable of both obedience and contempt.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex conditional arguments regarding God's goodness, prescience, and power. Pass A preserves the Latin syntax and nuances (e.g., 'species' as 'species/attributes', 'substantia' as 'substance'), and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the logical causal relations and theological distinctions. Scripture references are handled correctly via the text's internal logic.
